name: Dreadmaxxing

card.summary: Growing and styling dreadlocks (locs) in a thick, full-head, textured form as a hair-based way to raise perceived attractiveness.
card.note: Heavy or tightly installed locs can strain the hair and scalp, and some workplaces and schools have treated locs as unprofessional.

quick.overview:
Dreadmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for deliberately growing and styling dreadlocks so that the hair itself becomes a feature of the face and overall look. Practitioners treat the locs as a style asset: fullness across the whole head, even thickness, visible texture and length are the qualities they aim for.

The approach rests on style and personal presentation rather than on any medical treatment. No published study has tested whether particular loc styles change ratings of attractiveness; the practice draws on long cultural traditions of locs and on community opinion about which versions look best.
quick.how: People who follow the idea describe starting from healthy, well-conditioned hair, choosing a starting method suited to their hair type (such as twisting, backcombing or crocheting), and giving the locs months to mature while keeping the scalp clean. Fans of the style talk about a full-head layout instead of a high top, a moderate thickness, some texture, length past the shoulders and sometimes colored strands. Maturing typically takes many months to years.
quick.risks: Very heavy locs can cause neck strain, and hair that is pulled tightly or dyed while unhealthy can break or thin. Locs are sometimes judged as unprofessional, and anti-hair-discrimination laws such as the US CROWN Act were passed because of reported job and school consequences.

lead: Dreadmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for growing and styling dreadlocks (also called locs or dreads) in the way practitioners believe is most attractive. Hair is one of the few features that can be changed freely, and followers of the idea treat the loc style as a way to frame the face, add visual interest and signal a distinct personal look.

Dreadlocks are rope-like strands of hair. They can form naturally in very curly or coily hair or be created by twisting, backcombing or crocheting, and they differ from matting that results from neglect or damage [1]. They have a long history: locked hair appears in ancient records, including a roughly 4,000-year-old lock from Sudan, and the Rastafari movement spread the style worldwide through reggae and later hip-hop [1].

Within the community, the term is associated with a set of aesthetic preferences about what a good set of locs looks like: a full head of locs rather than a high top, moderate thickness, visible texture, healthy hang and substantial length. These preferences come from forum opinion; no published research has compared loc styles for attractiveness. Reported downsides include weight on the neck, hair damage if styled or colored while unhealthy, and bias in some workplaces and schools [1].

chain: Install and mature locs in a full, even, textured layout
Hair frames the face and becomes a distinctive style feature
angle.text: Locs change the silhouette and texture of the hair itself, so the look is immediate once they are installed and mature. Practitioners aim for full-head coverage, even thickness and length because they say these details separate polished locs from sparse or frizzy ones.

paras: In looksmaxxing usage, dreadmaxxing means treating dreadlocks as an optimisation project. Locs are rope-like sections of hair that lock together over time, and people can start them with several methods depending on hair type [1]. Followers say not all locs look equally good and discuss the differences in terms of thickness, density, hang, texture and length.

Typical community criteria for attractive locs are a full-head layout (not a high top or a small number of thick locs), a moderate thickness, visible texture that makes each loc look distinct, length of at least shoulder or chest level, and healthy hair as the base. Some also mention dyeing selected strands for contrast.

Locs are far older than the looksmaxxing label. Wikipedia notes that locked hair appears in ancient Egyptian and Minoan depictions and in a roughly 4,000-year-old lock from the Kerma culture in Sudan [1]. In Senegal the Baye Fall movement, founded in 1887, is known for its locs, and Rastafari in Jamaica adopted them in the twentieth century [1].
In the African diaspora, locs have often expressed Black pride and resistance to Eurocentric beauty standards [1]. Looksmaxxing communities use the term in a styling sense and borrow the aesthetic.

Locs are sometimes viewed as unprofessional, and some Black people have reported being fired or not hired because of them [1]. The CROWN Act, first passed in California in 2019, bans hair discrimination, and by 2023 twenty-four US states had passed similar laws [1]. Forum users also raise this issue themselves, asking about situations where locs could be judged improper.

Very heavy locs can cause neck pain and limited mobility, and religious practices that forbid washing or cutting locs have been linked to health problems [1]. Community guides stress that hair health comes first, and say that dyeing carries more risk when hair is already weak. Hair that is pulled tightly can be strained by installation and retightening.

timeline.event: A roughly 4,000-year-old lock from the Kerma culture in Sudan is among the earliest locked hair recorded [1].
The Baye Fall movement in Senegal, known for locs, is founded [1].
Reggae's popularity spreads locs worldwide; hip-hop later carries the style further [1].
California passes the first CROWN Act banning hair discrimination [1].

lore.intro: On looksmaxxing forums, dreadmaxxing guides rank locs by quality and argue that a well-made set improves appeal, while some users question how locs are perceived socially.

claims.claim: A full, textured, long set of locs adds more appeal than sparse or high-top locs
claims.believers: Forum guide authors sort locs into weaker, middling and strong tiers and say fullness, texture and length separate them.
claims.experts: No published study has compared loc styles for attractiveness; research on locs mostly covers cultural history and workplace discrimination [1].

claims.claim: Healthy hair is the foundation of long, thick locs
claims.believers: Guides say hair health determines how long and thick locs can get and warn about dyeing weak hair.
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that matting from neglect or damage differs from locs and that very heavy locs can strain the neck [1].

claims.claim: Locs can cost social or professional standing
claims.believers: Some forum users worry locs read as improper or are linked with stereotypes.
claims.experts: Reports cited by Wikipedia describe job and school consequences, which led to the CROWN Act and similar laws [1].
